doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Teagarden, the Army and the radio repair trade, then Ralph Flanagan
summary: Discovering Jack Teagarden, uncertain direction, a father-advised radio repair trade, National Guard band, and the call from John Strophe leading to joining Ralph Flanagan.

bands.name: Red Nichols and His Five Pennies

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Let me skip up to when you made the move to New Orleans and what happened in that period in your life?

Okay. Well I’ll just briefly say that trombone became my favorite instrument. I played the violin all the way through high school and even a little with the local symphony afterwards. But trombone became my favorite and I eventually dropped the violin all together. And my father brought home a record from his place where he worked, and it was a Red Nichols and the Five Pennies recording. And on that record was Jack Teagarden. That was my first introduction to the sound of Jack Teagarden. And this was about 1947 I guess. Well I fell in love with his style right away. Now from the years where I got out of high school and I went in the Army and spent a couple of years in the Army, and during the period when I was about 18 years old until about 25, I was kind of mentally going back and forth between what was considered bebop music and Dixieland music and swing music — sort of three different styles there. So at that point I really didn’t know exactly what I wanted to play, and I didn’t even know if I was going to be a professional musician or not. As a matter of fact I learned another trade, through the suggestion of my father. He said, “Music is great, but you ought to learn something else in case the music goes sour.” So I learned to be a radio and television repairman. I went to school in Chicago. But then I worked for Motorola and I played music at night in Quincy. Well then I went in the Army in 1952, and spent 18 months in the National © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Guard from Illinois, and I was in the Division band, the marching band. Then when I got out of the Army I went to work as a radio repairman in a local shop and playing music at night. Finally in 1955 I got a phone call and it was a man by the name of John Strophe. Ten years before this John and I were students in a music camp, Interlochen Music Camp in Michigan. Well we never corresponded after that. And here ten years had elapsed and he was playing with the Ralph Flanagan Orchestra, traveling through Quincy doing a concert. And he called me and he said, “I remembered that this was your home town.” And so he picked me out of the phone book and called me and said, “I’d love to see you again, come down and listen to our concert.” And they were putting on a concert at the local high school where I had played many times. So I went down and found out that they were looking for an extra trombone man in the band. Of course he had already said, “Why don’t you bring your horn” not knowing what he had in mind. Well music was always a great interest at that point and so Mr. Flanagan asked me if I would play a few songs for him, that I’d been recommended by John Strophe. So I played a few tunes with the piano and he liked my playing so much he said, “Would you join my band?” And it took me just a few seconds to decide. I thought well I really would rather play music. So I left Quincy in ‘55 and joined Ralph Flanagan in Texas in November, and that was the beginning of my professional career. It was a big band, it was a popular band in the early 50s. And I played with him and the first stop after about a month was in New Orleans, after touring Texas. We played an engagement at the Roosevelt Hotel in New Orleans and at that point I had already realized that Dixieland was my favorite kind of jazz music. And it’s what I felt like I did the best at. So I could hardly wait to get through work at the hotel and go on Bourbon Street, and I brought my horn with me and I listened to as many bands as I could in the course of a few evenings. And they asked me to sit in and play. I got acquainted with George Gerard and his band he called the New Orleans Five. I sat in with the band and after I finished playing he offered me a job. And it was my second night in New Orleans.
